\title{\bfseries Rules That Stop Working\\
\large Why feedback institutions survive shocks to the world but not shocks to their own
instruments, and what it takes to notice}

\author{}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent
A standing policy rule---``restrict activity whenever the indicator crosses this threshold''---is a
feedback device, and feedback devices are unexpectedly robust. When the world worsens, the indicator
rises, the rule fires more often, and the institution keeps doing roughly the right thing without
anyone revisiting the statute. We show computationally that this robustness has a sharp boundary,
and that the boundary is not where the literature on institutional adaptation usually looks.

Using a simulated polity governing an endemic epidemic, we separate two kinds of structural break.
When the \emph{environment} changes---the pathogen becomes more transmissible---a rule calibrated
before the change remains within one percent of the best rule available after it. There is
essentially nothing for adaptation to do. When the \emph{instrument} changes---the same restriction
now delivers a quarter of the behavioural response while costing what it always cost---the pre-shock
rule carries a large excess burden, and its feedback structure makes matters worse rather than
better: rising prevalence causes it to intervene harder, buying less each time. The correct response
is not to stop governing but to \emph{substitute}: hold the instrument that still works and stop
paying for the one that broke.

We also show that what a stale rule costs \emph{factors}, into a part recoverable only by an
authority that notices and revises, and a part recoverable by having legislated a better rule in the
first place. The distinction has teeth: in two of the four polities we calibrate, the stale rule
costs $18$--$44\%$ while the adaptive part is worth nothing at all. An authority evaluated there
looks rigid while facing no adaptive problem, and the reform it would be prescribed---faster review,
more responsiveness, better monitoring---is the wrong one.

We then ask what an authority must be able to observe to notice. We give a policy-maker---instantiated
as a language model that writes its rules as short executable expressions, so that every enacted
policy is a legible, archivable artifact---a governing loop equipped with different informational
channels, and vary them factorially: a compliance channel reporting rule violations, a monitoring
channel reporting the realized performance of the policy actually in force, and an institutional
memory of precedents. \ResultsAbstractSentence

The design implication is specific. Auditing whether a rule was followed cannot reveal that the rule
has stopped working; only evaluating what the rule achieved can. Institutions built to detect
non-compliance are, in a precise and measurable sense, blind to instrument failure.
\end{abstract}

\section{The problem: when is a rule stale?}

Institutions govern through standing rules. A central bank follows a reaction function, a health
authority a threshold for restrictions, a regulator a trigger for intervention. Writing the rule
down is the point: it makes the state's behaviour predictable, reviewable, and contestable in a way
that discretionary case-by-case action is not---the constraint \emph{is} the product
\citep{north1990institutions}, and the classical argument for issuing a standing rule at all is that
the commitment is worth more than the flexibility it costs \citep{kydland1977rules}.

The institutional literature has a name for what happens next: \emph{drift}, in which a rule is left
formally intact while the environment moves out from under it and its impact quietly collapses
\citep{hacker2004privatizing,mahoney2010gradual}. Drift is this paper's object, and the model below is
a drift generator with a known ground truth---the rule is untouched, the world moves, and we can
price exactly what the rule's survival cost.

The standard worry about such rules is that they go stale, and the canonical statement of the worry
is Lucas's: a relation estimated under one policy regime need not survive the introduction of
another \citep{lucas1976critique}, with Goodhart's \citeyearpar{goodhart1984monetary} corollary that
a measure targeted by policy ceases to be a good measure. Both are usually read as warnings about
\emph{estimation}. We want to read them as a question about \emph{institutional design}: given that
a rule will eventually stop working, what does the institution enforcing it have to be able to see
in order to find out?

This paper makes three moves. First, we show that ``the rule goes stale'' is far too coarse: the
staleness of a feedback rule depends on \emph{which part of the world moved}, and for one large
class of movements the rule barely goes stale at all. Second, we identify the class that does break
it---changes to the efficacy of the instrument the rule operates---and show why a feedback structure
converts that change from a nuisance into an active harm. Third, we vary the informational
architecture around a rule-writing authority and measure which channel is load-bearing for
detection.

\subsection{Why a computational model, and what it is for}

We use a simulation because the question is counterfactual in a way historical policy episodes
cannot be: we need to know how well the \emph{best available} rule would have performed after a
break in order to say whether an authority's response was good, and no observed polity provides
that. Our claim is not that the simulation predicts what any real health authority would do
\citep[a claim that would require far more than statistical realism;][]{li2026statistical}, but that
it isolates a mechanism and bounds it---the exploratory, mechanism-isolating use that a recent review
of the LLM-versus-human comparison evidence argues is currently the defensible one
\citep{anthis2025position}.

The policy-maker in our model is a large language model. We use it not as a claim about how humans
reason---the silicon-sampling programme, which asks whether a language model can stand in for a human
population \citep{argyle2023out}, is not what we are doing---but as a convenient generator of
\emph{written rules}: it must express its policy as a short executable expression, which means every
decision it takes leaves an inspectable artifact and its revision history is measurable. Where prior
work has language models set a tax rate, fill in a fixed policy schema
\citep{wang2025taxagent,li2023econagent,decurto2026narratives}, or take repeated \emph{actions} on a
shared resource and be scored on whether the resource survives \citep{piatti2024govsim}, here the
object the authority produces is the rule itself---a structured statement with a condition and a
prescribed aim \citep{crawford1995grammar}, not a scalar. That is what makes questions like ``did the
institution revise its policy, and in which direction'' answerable at all.

\section{The model}
\label{sec:model-social}

A full specification following the ODD protocol
\citep{grimm2006odd,grimm2010oddupdate,grimm2020odd} is in \cref{app:odd}; the verification and
calibration evidence is documented separately, in the manner of TRACE \citep{grimm2014trace}. The
essentials follow.\footnote{We use \emph{feedback} throughout in the control-theoretic sense: a
standing rule keyed to a measured indicator. This is not policy feedback in the political-science
sense, in which an enacted policy reshapes the coalitions and interests that later act on it
\citep{pierson2000increasing}. Our authority faces no constituency and no switching cost, which is
what makes the lock-in reported in \cref{sec:lockin-social} a narrower and stranger finding.}

\paragraph{The governed system.} A population is partitioned into susceptible, infectious, and
recovered shares \citep{kermack1927contribution}. Immunity wanes and a small number of cases arrive
from outside, so the disease is \emph{endemic}: it does not burn out and cannot be waited out. This
is a substantive modelling choice rather than a technical one. In a model where the epidemic ends by
itself, ``do nothing until it is over'' is a viable strategy, and the interesting governance question
disappears.

\paragraph{The authority.} At regular review points the authority promulgates a standing rule
governing two costed instruments, restriction intensity and vaccination effort. The rule is applied
every period until replaced, not re-decided each period---an institution issuing a standing rule
rather than an administrator making daily calls. It is scored on infection burden plus a weight
$\lambda$ times intervention cost.

$\lambda$ is the polity's political economy in one number: the price it places on a unit of
restriction relative to a unit of illness. It is not a nuisance parameter to be marginalized. Set it
low and permanent maximal restriction is optimal; set it high and doing nothing is; and in both
cases the optimum sits at a corner where no shock can move it. Only at intermediate values does the
polity face a genuine trade-off, and only then can it be said to adapt at all. We report the whole
range (\cref{fig:surface}) rather than a single calibration.

\paragraph{The break.} At the midpoint of the horizon, without announcement, the efficacy of
restriction falls to a quarter: the same order produces a quarter of the behavioural change, while
costing exactly what it did before. Compliance fatigue is the obvious reading. Crucially,
\textbf{efficacy is never observable}. The authority sees prevalence, its own past choices, and
whatever its institutional memory retains. It never sees the parameter connecting them.

\section{Measuring what adaptation could be worth}
\label{sec:headroom-social}

Comparative claims about institutional adaptation are usually made against a single reference: the
policy that was in force before. That reference tells us whether an authority changed course
profitably. It cannot tell us whether changing course was worth much, and without that, a finding of
``no adaptation effect'' is uninterpretable---it may be a fact about the authority or a fact about
the situation.

We therefore calibrate two references inside one shared vocabulary of rules. The \emph{frozen} rule
is the best rule available given everything knowable before the break, held unchanged through it.
The \emph{clairvoyant} rule is the best rule in the same vocabulary given the break already known.
They differ in exactly one respect: when they were allowed to look. The ratio of their post-break
burdens is the \emph{adaptation headroom}, and it is the entire prize any adapting authority is
competing for.

\subsection{Two remedies, routinely conflated}
\label{sec:two-remedies}

One ratio is not enough, and the reason is a distinction with direct institutional consequences.
Write $\pi_{\mathrm{fixed}}$ for the best \emph{standing} rule over the whole broken horizon, chosen
with hindsight. Then what the stale rule costs factors:
\begin{equation}
\underbrace{\frac{L(\pi_{\mathrm{frozen}})}{L(\pi_{\mathrm{switch}})}}_{\text{staleness}}
=
\underbrace{\frac{L(\pi_{\mathrm{fixed}})}{L(\pi_{\mathrm{switch}})}}_{\text{adaptation headroom}}
\times
\underbrace{\frac{L(\pi_{\mathrm{frozen}})}{L(\pi_{\mathrm{fixed}})}}_{\text{robustness headroom}} .
\end{equation}

Staleness is the quantity the literature on institutional rigidity reports: the old rule is worse
now than it was. But it does not say what to do about it. The adaptation term is the part recoverable
\emph{only} by an authority that notices and revises. The robustness term is the part recoverable by
having written a different rule in the first place---by a legislature, not a regulator, and before
the fact rather than after.

Neither term is our invention, and the second in particular has a home. It is the institutional
counterpart of choosing a rule to perform acceptably across a set of models rather than optimally
within one \citep{hansen2008robustness}, and of the finding inside monetary policy proper that a rule
tuned to a single model does poorly in the others \citep{levin1999robustness}. What the factorization
adds is that the two are separately \emph{measurable} in a given polity, before any authority is
observed---which is what lets one ask which of the two remedies a particular break actually calls
for.

We measure two cases where these separate completely, and they separate along different axes. Under
\emph{total} instrument failure at the baseline price, the stale rule costs $1.18\times$ and the
adaptation headroom is $1.01\times$. Holding the break at its baseline severity and raising the
\emph{price} of intervention instead, the stale rule costs $1.44\times$ and the adaptation headroom
is exactly $1.00\times$. In both, the best standing rule is effectively the same before and after
the break: nothing needed to change, the wrong rule had been written. An authority evaluated in
either would appear rigid while in fact facing no adaptive problem at all, and the reform it would
be prescribed---greater responsiveness, faster review cycles, better monitoring---would be the wrong
reform.

We report both because our first version varied severity and price \emph{together} and would have
credited the whole effect to severity. Separating them is what makes the claim a controlled one, and
it strengthened rather than weakened it: the finding holds along each axis by itself.

Notably, this is not what we expected. The severe regime was added on the assumption that a harsher
break leaves more for adaptation to recover. Measuring it says the opposite: past a point, the
failure is complete enough that a single robust rule dominates, and responsiveness buys nothing.

\begin{takeaway}
``This rule is costly'' and ``this rule must change'' are different diagnoses. Only the second is a
case for a more attentive government, and staleness alone cannot tell them apart.
\end{takeaway}

\subsection{The first result: which shocks a rule shrugs off}

\Cref{tab:headroom} and \cref{fig:surface} carry the paper's first finding. A shock to the
\emph{environment}---a more transmissible pathogen---leaves headroom of essentially one. The
pre-break rule remains near-optimal after the break, and no authority, however attentive, could have
demonstrated an improvement.

The reason is that a threshold rule is a feedback device. The shock raises prevalence; prevalence is
the variable the rule keys on; so the rule fires more often, entirely on its own. The institution
adapts without anyone adapting it, because the indicator still means what it meant.

A shock to the \emph{instrument} is different in kind. Nothing in the indicator reveals that a unit
of restriction now buys less, so no threshold on that indicator recovers the right behaviour. Worse,
the feedback structure that was protective before is now actively harmful: prevalence rises, so the
rule restricts harder, so the polity pays more for a fraction of the effect. The correct response is
to \emph{stop}, which is precisely the response the rule's own logic forbids.

The distinction between uncertainty about the \emph{state} and uncertainty about the \emph{policy
multiplier} has a fifty-year pedigree in policy design, and so does its normative implication: an
authority whose instrument has weakened should attenuate \citep{brainard1967uncertainty}. What we add
is the observation that a feedback rule keyed to the state does the opposite automatically.

\begin{takeaway}
Feedback rules are robust to shocks in the governed system and fragile to shocks in the governing
instrument. The robustness and the fragility have the same cause.
\end{takeaway}

\subsection{Is this a fact about epidemics, or about institutions?}
\label{sec:library-social}

A reasonable objection to everything above is that it describes a pathogen. Compartmental models have
a particular structure, and a finding that depends on it is epidemiology rather than political
science. We therefore repeated the identical measurement on a library of polities with nothing
mechanically in common: a central bank governing by policy rate, a platform governing discourse by
content moderation, a fishing community governing a stock by quota and reserve---the common-pool setting in which
rules-in-use, monitoring and rule revision are themselves the object of analysis
\citep{ostrom1990governing}---a firm governing
inventory by order quantity, and a treasury governing demand by tax and transfer. Each receives the
same kind of break---its principal instrument quietly loses efficacy---and each is scored against
three references calibrated in its own institutional vocabulary.

\input{generated/library_table}

The result is that scarcity, not headroom, is the normal condition. Across \libWorlds{} polities only
\libOverEleven{} leave adaptation worth more than a tenth of the incumbent rule's cost. For most of
them, an authority that watched carefully and revised promptly would have been indistinguishable from
one that legislated once and went home---not because attentiveness is worthless in general, but
because in those worlds the better answer was available at the outset to anyone who thought harder
about the rule.

This is an uncomfortable finding for a literature that treats responsiveness as an unqualified
institutional virtue, and we think it is the more useful one. It says that the case for adaptive
governance is not general; it is conditional on a property of the domain that can be measured in
advance, cheaply, without observing any government at all. Monetary policy reached a version of this
conclusion by a different route: a rule chosen for robustness across models often beats one optimized
within the model believed at the time \citep{levin1999robustness}. What we add is the measurement, in
domains where no such literature exists to consult.

Two of the polities are worth naming because they fail in instructive ways. The treasury cannot host
the experiment at all: in its configuration the optimal tax rate is zero---the economy reaches
potential from accumulated household balances, so taxation only distorts---and the shock enters as a
collapse in \emph{compliance}, which multiplies the rate. A collapse in the enforcement of a tax
nobody should be levying is arithmetically nothing. The firm is a genuine negative result about a
whole family of shocks: a lengthened supply lead time, which one might expect to punish a stale
ordering rule, is absorbed almost entirely, because an order-up-to rule with a free target answers a
longer lag by simply holding more. Both are reported rather than dropped, which is the point of
running a library instead of a flagship.

The polity with the most to gain from attentiveness is the central bank, and the \emph{shape} of the
three institutions is the substance. The incumbent rule leans hard against inflation from a high
neutral rate. The best possible \emph{fixed} answer to a collapse in monetary transmission is to stop
leaning altogether and hold a constant rate---an institution that abandons feedback, structurally the
same move as switching to a rule that does not depend on the quantity that moved
\citep{orphanides2002robust}. The clairvoyant
authority does neither: it keeps leaning, at half the strength, while moving its whole rate path down
to the zero lower bound. What adaptation buys here is not a change in the \emph{rule} but a change in
the \emph{level} at which the rule operates, and no re-tuning of the incumbent's thresholds can
express it. This is Lucas's critique of policy evaluation \citep{lucas1976critique} recovered as a
measurement rather than argued as a principle.

\begin{takeaway}
The case for adaptive governance is domain-conditional, and the condition is measurable before any
government is observed. In most of the polities we built, a better standing rule---not a more
attentive authority---was what the situation called for.
\end{takeaway}

\section{An authority that will not put an instrument down}
\label{sec:priors-social}

The clearest failure we observed did not occur in the epidemic. It occurred in the central bank, and
our first reading of it was wrong in a way worth setting out, because the correction is the finding.

Recall the structure: transmission of the policy rate to the economy collapses at the break, so a
point of interest rate buys a fraction of the behavioural response it used to buy while costing what
it always cost. The clairvoyant institution cuts to near the zero lower bound and holds there. The
incumbent Taylor rule \citep{taylor1993discretion}, which leans against inflation, instead sees prices
drifting and raises rates.

Our language-model authority did worse than the incumbent rule. It set an average post-break rate of
$9.51$, against the frozen rule's $7.40$ and the clairvoyant's $1.53$, for a total loss of $3891$
against $1871$---worse than every scripted comparison in the study, including an authority that holds
the neutral rate and never acts.

The revealing number is not the loss but its decomposition. This authority achieved the \emph{best
inflation and output stabilization of any arm in the experiment}, outperforming the clairvoyant
institution on the mandate's first objective. It simply spent three times as much doing so, holding a
restrictive stance long after restriction had stopped restricting anything.

This is superstitious learning in Levitt and March's sense \citep{levitt1988organizational}: the
authority receives compelling evidence that its actions are working---the objective it can watch is
moving in the right direction---while the break has severed the connection between action and outcome
that the evidence is being read against.

Its instructions stated, at every review, that the rate's cost is charged ``whether or not the rate
reaches the economy''. It read that and leaned harder. That is the exact inverse of the classical
prescription for a weakened instrument \citep{brainard1967uncertainty}, which makes the behaviour a
departure from a stated benchmark rather than a deviation from an ad hoc one.

\subsection{The explanation we expected, and why it is wrong}

The natural reading is that the authority knew too much: a prior about what central banks do, strong
enough to survive a written instruction designed to displace it. We committed to that reading in
advance, and to the experiment that could refute it---the identical economy with every economic name
removed, so that the same control problem arrives without announcing its domain. Inflation became
\emph{signal A}, the policy rate became \emph{a lever}, and the mandate was rewritten in the same
neutral vocabulary. If familiarity caused the failure, anonymity should have relieved it.

It did not. The disguised authority scored $4016$ against $3891$: no better, and if anything slightly
worse, with the difference well inside the range attributable to chance.

Three checks rule out the comfortable ways of setting that aside. The disguise genuinely concealed
the domain---across four hundred disguised briefings there is not one occurrence of \emph{inflation},
\emph{central bank}, \emph{Taylor} or \emph{output gap}, against twenty-five thousand
occurrences of the first word alone in the paired condition. The disguise also genuinely worked on
the authority's \emph{reasoning}: the share of rules written in recognizable Taylor form falls from
$82\%$ to $22\%$. And yet the behaviour that constitutes the failure does not follow. The post-break
rate moves from $9.51$ to $9.12$, against a gap of more than eight points to the clairvoyant policy.
In all forty runs across both conditions, not one authority brings its post-break rate below the best
constant rate available to it. Neither version withdraws.

Removing the textbook removed the textbook and left the failure standing.

We should be exact about how much this settles, because the honest version is narrower than ``the
authority's expertise was irrelevant''. Two qualifications. The experiment can rule out an expertise
effect worth more than about a fifth of the failure; below roughly a tenth it cannot see one at all,
and the tightest statement it supports is that anonymity was worth \emph{at most} four percent of the
authority's excess cost. And stripping the domain did not leave the authority with no preconceptions
---it left it with different ones, in some respects more aggressive: the neutral authority leaned on
its indicator harder than the central bank did, and never once resorted to simply fixing the lever at
a constant, which the informed authority did twenty-five times. What the comparison measures is
therefore the difference between two sets of preconceptions rather than the effect of having any. On
some narrower readings expertise does show: the disguised authority ends its run at a lower rate
($8.91$ against $10.51$), which is the direction the expertise story predicts, even though it does not
end up cheaper overall.

\subsection{What is actually going on}

The failure is not that the authority knows what central banks do. It is that it will not put down an
instrument that has stopped working, whatever the instrument is called. It optimises the objective it
can watch moving---inflation, or \emph{signal A}---and treats the price of intervention as a charge to
be absorbed rather than as a reason to stop intervening. Told explicitly that the charge accrues even
when the lever does nothing, it pays and continues.

That is a more general claim than the one we set out to make, and a more uncomfortable one for the
design of automated authority. A domain-specific failure could be addressed by domain-specific
briefing: warn the system about this economy, this instrument, this history. A general unwillingness
to abandon a costly instrument cannot, because the warning was already there and was already read.

\begin{takeaway}
We expected an authority that failed because it knew too much. What we measured is an authority that
fails because it will not stop---and stripping away everything it knew about the domain left the
failure exactly where it was.
\end{takeaway}

\section{Precedent without evaluation produces lock-in}
\label{sec:lockin-social}

Before turning to which channel lets an authority \emph{detect} instrument failure, we report the
clearest behavioural finding in the study, because it concerns a piece of institutional machinery
that is usually assumed benign.

Political science has a name for arrangements that survive past their usefulness because operating
them raises the cost of switching \citep{pierson2000increasing}. What follows is a stripped-down
instance: no coalition, no sunk cost, no constituency---only the availability of the institution's own
past decisions---and it is sufficient. The nearest survey of this machinery in the artificial-agent
literature reports neither the degradation nor the mechanism we find \citep{jiang2026anatomy}.

We gave the rule-writing authority an institutional memory: at each review it is shown the most
similar past situations it has faced, what rule it enacted then, and how that turned out. This is
precedent, in the ordinary administrative sense. The implementation is the standard one---a memory
stream of past episodes, retrieved by similarity to the current situation and inserted into
deliberation \citep{park2023generative}---which matters for how the result reads: what follows is a
failure mode of the widely adopted memory architecture, not of a bespoke one. It is the channel one
would expect to help most across a structural break, since a break is exactly the situation in which
the past is informative about what no longer works.

It was the only channel that made the authority measurably \emph{worse}, and the reason is not that
it supplied bad precedent. We measured how often the authority actually revised the law in force:

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
what the authority could see & revisions per review & distinct rules per run \\
\midrule
nothing & $0.85$ & $14.4$ \\
compliance reporting only & $0.86$ & $14.5$ \\
outcome monitoring only & $0.77$ & $8.2$ \\
\textbf{precedent only} & $\mathbf{0.08}$ & $\mathbf{2.1}$ \\
precedent $+$ outcome monitoring & $0.64$ & $7.2$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

An authority shown its own precedents stops revising: it changes the law at $8\%$ of reviews instead
of $85\%$, and spends the whole run alternating between about two rules rather than exploring
fourteen. We checked the obvious explanation---that precedent drawn from before the break actively
misleads---and it is not supported: only $39.6\%$ of the precedents retrieved after the break dated
from before it, against a chance baseline near $69\%$. Retrieval was, if anything, biased towards
recent cases. The mechanism is simpler and less comfortable. Shown what it did last time, the
authority does it again. Precedent does not have to be wrong to be harmful; it only has to be
\emph{available}---a competency trap in Levitt and March's sense \citep{levitt1988organizational},
and the reason we ruled out the misleading-precedent explanation before reaching for it.

The collapse from fourteen distinct rules to two is a collapse in exploration, and March's account
predicts its consequence precisely: exploitation refines faster and pays sooner, and is
self-destructive when the environment moves \citep{march1991exploration}.

The remedy is visible in the same table, and it is specific. Adding outcome monitoring to a
precedent-equipped authority restores most of the revision it had suppressed ($0.08 \to 0.64$), and
the interaction is statistically the largest term in our design ($+0.338$, $95\%$ CI
$[+0.287, +0.387]$, $p_{\text{Holm}}=0.0007$). Precedent tells an institution what it did; evaluation
tells it that what it did has stopped working. The first alone is a machine for continuity. Only the
pair is a machine for learning.

In Argyris and Sch\"on's vocabulary, precedent alone supports single-loop learning---error correction
\emph{within} the standing rule, the thermostat's kind of learning---while the question of whether the
standing rule should still be in force is double-loop and requires the evaluation channel
\citep{argyris1978organizational}. That their own worked example of single-loop learning is a
thermostat, which is precisely a threshold feedback rule, is not a coincidence we can take credit
for; but our two behavioural measures, revisions per review and distinct rules per run, are an
operationalization of double-loop capacity.

One caution, which we state because the obvious policy reading of the table above is wrong. Across
the eight informational regimes, more revision goes with lower loss ($r = -0.82$), and it would be
natural to conclude that authorities should revise more. Our own data does not support that. When we
remove both the regime effect and the difficulty of the particular epidemic each run faced, the
association between how often \emph{a given run} revised and how well it did falls to $-0.11$, which
at this sample size is indistinguishable from nothing. An authority that happened to legislate more
often within a fixed informational setting did not thereby govern better.

So revision is not the good thing, and there is a principled case for an authority that declines to
revise precisely when circumstances appear to warrant it \citep{kydland1977rules}. What separates our
case from that one is that we measured the headroom first: adaptation here is worth $1.19\times$, so
revision \emph{was} warranted, and the failure to revise is a failure rather than a commitment. What
the memory channel removed was the \emph{capacity} for revision---the institution stopped being the
kind of thing that could change its mind---and that is what cost it. Prescribing ``revise more
often'' would be treating a symptom that is not, on its own, the mechanism.

\begin{takeaway}
Institutional memory did not misinform our authority---it stopped it from reconsidering. Precedent
and evaluation are complements, and precedent deployed without evaluation is worse than no
institutional memory at all. But the remedy is the evaluation channel, not a quota of revisions.
\end{takeaway}

This is a claim about a simulated authority, and we are careful not to inflate it into a claim about
courts or bureaucracies. What the model licenses is narrower and still useful: it identifies a
mechanism---availability of one's own past decisions suppressing revision---that is measurable, that
has a measurable antidote, and that would be invisible to any evaluation reporting only whether the
polity did well.

\section{What must an institution see?}
\label{sec:channels-social}

If instrument failure is the case that matters, the design question becomes concrete: what
information does an authority need in order to detect one? We equip the rule-writing authority with
different channels and vary them factorially. Each is a recognizable piece of institutional
machinery.

The two are not more and less of one thing called monitoring. Behn separates the \emph{control}
purpose of performance measurement---did subordinates do what was specified---from the \emph{learn}
purpose---why is performance what it is---and shows that the two demand different measures
\citep{behn2003measure}. We treat them as separate factors for that reason, and the factorial is what
turns the distinction into a testable one. It also sharpens our own earlier complaint: on Behn's
account ``better monitoring'' is not one lever, so a reform package that bundles them is not one
reform.


\begin{description}[leftmargin=0em,style=nextline]
\item[Compliance reporting] The authority learns when its instructions were rejected or
malformed---the analogue of an enforcement or legal-validity channel. It reports on the
\emph{form} of the rule and says nothing about its consequences: a procedural agency in Wilson's
typology, where outputs are observable and outcomes are not \citep{wilson1989bureaucracy}. An
authority issuing valid rules receives, correctly, no information from it at all.
\item[Outcome monitoring] The authority learns what its currently standing rule actually achieved
over the last review period, and retains the preceding entries. This is monitoring and evaluation in
the ordinary administrative sense. It is the only channel in which an unobservable instrument
failure leaves any trace, and the trace is indirect: two consecutive reviews reading ``same policy,
worse result''. Monitoring of the resource itself, and not only of the appropriators, is the feature
Ostrom found in long-enduring commons institutions and the one our compliance channel deliberately
omits \citep{ostrom1990governing}.
\item[Institutional memory] Retrieved precedent---the most similar past situations and what was done
then. Valuable for recurring problems and, across a structural break, potentially misleading, since
the most similar past situation may belong to a regime that no longer exists.
\end{description}

Stating the prediction in advance, and asymmetrically: monitoring should carry the effect;
compliance reporting should do nothing here; memory may be neutral or actively harmful across the
break. The full pre-registration, including the conditions under which we would withdraw rather than
adjust the claim, was committed before the treatment runs.

\subsection{What the authority actually wrote}

Because policy here is code rather than a number, the enacted rules can simply be read.
\Cref{tab:crossmodel} reports whether the ordering replicates across the language models we could
access; more informative for a reader is the content of the rules themselves. Three observations
recur.

Authorities with no informational channel at all overwhelmingly emit \emph{constants}---a fixed
restriction level with no reference to the state of the epidemic. This is not a novel or creative
policy; it is a degenerate one, less responsive than the threshold rules the references use. An
authority with nothing to learn from does not merely fail to adapt: it never engages with the
situation in the first place.

Authorities with monitoring converge instead on \emph{proportional} rules, restricting in proportion
to prevalence. This form lies outside the threshold vocabulary the clairvoyant reference was
optimized within, which is a caution as much as a result---an authority that outperforms the
reference by writing a rule the reference could not express is telling us about our choice of
vocabulary. We therefore re-calibrate the clairvoyant reference over a widened vocabulary including
that form and report both comparisons.

Third, the direction of revision is measurable and it matters. An authority that responds to
worsening outcomes by restricting harder is failing in exactly the way the frozen rule fails, even
though it is nominally adapting.

\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{An audit of compliance is not an audit of efficacy.} The sharpest implication is
negative. A channel that reports whether rules were followed contains no information about whether
following them still accomplishes anything. These are different questions, and an institution
equipped only for the first is blind to instrument failure by construction rather than by
inattention. That is a claim about informational architecture, and it does not depend on the
authority being a language model: any decision procedure restricted to compliance data faces the
same wall.

\paragraph{Rules fail in the direction of their own logic.} A feedback rule does not fail by going
quiet. It fails by doing more of what it does, more expensively, in response to the deterioration it
is itself failing to prevent. Escalation is the diagnostic signature of instrument failure, and it
looks from the inside exactly like the rule working hard.

\paragraph{Adaptation is a category with boundaries.} \Cref{fig:surface} shows that most of the
parameter space we might have studied contains no adaptation problem: at a corner solution the
optimal rule is invariant to the shock. This is worth stating to a literature that routinely asks
whether agents, institutions, or organizations adapt without establishing that adapting was
available. A null result in a region with no headroom is not evidence of rigidity.

\paragraph{Policy as a readable artifact.} Requiring the authority to express itself in code is a
methodological choice with a payoff for social science specifically: the object of study becomes a
sequence of legible rules with a revision history, rather than a sequence of actions from which a
rule must be inferred. Questions about \emph{how} policy changed---abruptly or gradually, in form or
in parameter, toward escalation or withdrawal---become directly measurable.

\section{Limitations}

The model is a stylized governance setting, not an epidemiological or public-health one, and nothing
here is a recommendation about restrictions. The authority is a language model, which is a
convenient rule-writer and not a model of human deliberation; we make no claim that its failures
resemble human ones. Model access was limited to what was reachable without paid inference, biasing
the panel toward smaller systems. Following \citet{ye2026trails} we audit robustness at the level of
the environment and the protocol but do not systematically vary the wording in which the authority's
task is described. Finally, in the present regime the clairvoyant response is close to withdrawal;
a stronger version, in which a second instrument survives the break so that the correct response is
substitution rather than retreat, is specified and not yet run.

\section{Conclusion}

Institutions do not usually fail because their rules were wrong when written. They fail because the
world moved and nothing in the institution's information flow made that visible. We have tried to
make that intuition precise: to separate the movements a feedback rule quietly absorbs from those it
converts into escalating harm, to measure how much any given movement leaves worth adapting to, and
to identify which of an institution's informational channels can carry the news. The channel that
can is the one that asks what the policy achieved. The channel that cannot---and that institutions
build first---is the one that asks whether the policy was obeyed.
